div.p: Background/Aim: Glioblastoma is the most malignant brain tumor, and despite advances in treatment, survival rates are still dismal. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms of glioblastoma is needed. This study suggests potential therapeutic targets in glioblastoma that may provide new therapeutic insights. Materials and Methods: To identify hub genes in glioblastoma, three datasets were selected from the GEO database. After screening DEGs using GEO2R, GO and KEGG analyses were performed using DAVID. The PPI network was visualized using Cytoscape and 7 hub genes were extracted. The prognostic potential of 7 hub genes was investigated using the Gliovis and GEPIA2 databases. Results: In total, 176 up-regulated and 263 down-regulated genes were identified. From the PPI network, 7 hub genes were identified including CAMK2A, DLG4, SNAP25, SYT1, MYC, FN1, and VEGFA. Out of the 7 hub genes identified, FN1 and VEGFA have been associated with a poor prognosis in glioblastoma based on the survival analysis. Conclusion: This study suggests that high levels of FN1 and VEGFA expression are associated with a poor prognosis in glioblastoma and that both genes are promising targets for glioblastoma therapy. Bioinformatics analysis of DEGs revealed putative targets that might reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying glioblastoma.

Glioblastoma is the most aggressive glioma and a malignant brain tumor that occurs in approximately 3.26 people per 100,000 in the United States each year. Glioblastoma constitutes 14.2% of primary brain and other central nervous system tumors and 50.1% of primary malignant brain tumors (1). Currently, the standard treatment for glioblastoma patients includes a combination of maximally safe surgical resection, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, but median survival is only 8 months, and the 5-year survival rate is a dismal 6.9% (1, 2). The high mortality rate of glioblastoma underscores the need to identify the molecular mechanisms responsible. However, glioblastoma is a complex disease, and a variety of causes and factors are known to contribute to its progression. These factors include the tumor microenvironment, metabolic alterations, gene copy number variations, stem cell pathways, epigenetic modifications, gene fusions, and somatic mutations (3). Although many factors have been associated with the tumorigenesis of glioblastoma, the mechanisms by which these factors cause the tumors to grow and spread are not well understood. Early diagnosis and the identification of prognostic molecular biomarkers are essential for improving the survival rate and preventing glioblastoma (4-6), and thus, it is critical that the molecular, genetic, and metabolic characteristics of glioblastoma be fully understood so that improved prognostic assessment strategies are developed.

Gene expression profiling is a powerful tool that can be used to examine a variety of biological processes, such as cell differentiation, development, and disease progression, but can also be used to identify genes involved in a particular disease or condition, and thus, improve understanding of how genes function and are affected by diseases (7-10). Bioinformatics analysis can be used to identify potential biomarkers and pathways in a variety of tumors, including glioblastoma (11-13), and can also reveal complex biological mechanisms involved in diseases and potentially improve diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment (7, 14). Recent advances have allowed the identification of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), their molecular functions, and roles in 70
biological processes, including signaling pathways, which has led to a better understanding of the pathogeneses of diseases and provided a theoretical basis for early diagnosis and treatment (11,15).

In this study, we acquired glioblastoma-related RNA-seq and microarray data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. GEO2R and Venn Diagrams were used to identify significant DEGs. Gene Ontology (GO) analysis, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis, and protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis were then used to identify hub genes. This was followed by hub gene expression analysis and survival analysis to identify potential biomarkers.

div.head: Materials and Methods
div.p: Dataset source and screening of DEGs. We explored data from the National Center of Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GEO (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) for gene expression profiling studies (16). The inclusion criteria were expression studies that used microarray or RNA-seq and the use of samples pooled from normal brain and glioblastoma tissues. Only data from glioblastoma and normal brain tissues were included for further study; data from other gliomas, such as oligodendrogliomas, pilocytic astrocytomas, ependymomas, and medulloblastomas were excluded. As a result, we obtained glioblastoma-related microarray datasets GSE12657 and GSE50161 and RNA-seq dataset GSE147352. The GSE12657 dataset was generated using the GPL8300 platform and included 5 normal tissues and 7 glioblastoma tissues. The GSE50161 dataset was generated using the GPL570 platform and included 13 normal brain tissues and 34 glioblastoma tissues. The GSE147352 dataset was generated using the GPL20301 platform and included 15 normal brain tissues and 85 glioblastoma tissues. The online tool GEO2R (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/geo2r) was used to screen DEGs in glioblastoma and normal samples. The ggplot2 package (http://ggplot2.tidyverse.org) in R software was used to create a volcano plot of DEGs. Venn diagrams were generated using Bioinformatics and Evolutionary Genomics software (http://bioinformatics.psb.ugent.be/webtools/Venn).

div.head: Gene function and pathway enrichment analysis of DEGs.
div.p: The Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) (version 2021, https://david.ncifcrf.gov/home.jsp) (17) was used for GO analysis (http://geneontology.org/) (18,19), and KEGG pathway analysis (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/) (20-22) to investigate the potential functions of overlapped DEGs. GO terms were analyzed to identify 'Biological Processes', 'Cellular Components', and 'Molecular Functions' associated with DEGs. The KEGG database is a comprehensive resource for biological information that includes information on genes, proteins, pathways, and diseases. Additionally, dot plots were generated using the ggplot2 package in R software. p-Values <0.05 were considered to be statistically significant.

div.head: PPI network construction and hub gene determination.
div.p: The PPI network of overlapped DEGs was retrieved from the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes (STRING) (version 11.5, http://string-db.org) database and visualized using Cytoscape (version 3.9.1, http://cytoscape.org) software (23,24). To generate an interaction network, nodes with interaction scores greater than 0.40 (considered medium confidence) were included in the analysis. The Cytoscape plugin cytoHubba was used to explore hub genes based on 11 topological algorithms: Betweenness, Bottleneck, Closeness, Degree, Density of Maximum Neighborhood Component, EcCentricity, Edge Percolated Component, Maximal Clique Centrality, Maximum Neighborhood Component, Radiality, and Stress (25). To evaluate the functions of hub genes, a network of gene-gene interactions was constructed using GeneMANIA (http://genemania.org/) (26); a webbased platform that provides comprehensive information and analyzes gene functions and interactions.

div.head: Bioinformatics analysis of the clinical implications of hub genes.
div.p: The GlioVis (http://gliovis.bioinfo.cnio.es/) was used to evaluate the mRNA expression levels of screened hub genes (27). The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) glioblastoma datasets and Gliovis were employed to validate the expressions of identified hub genes. These datasets comprised 528 glioblastoma tumors and 10 non-tumor brain samples and contained HG-U133A RNA expression data. To validate the prognostic effects of the identified hub genes, survival analysis was conducted using Gene Expression Profiling Interactive Analysis (GEPIA2) (http://gepia2.cancer-pku.cn) (28). GEPIA2 performs this analysis using expression data obtained from the RNA sequencing of 9,736 tumor samples and 8,587 normal samples sourced from the TCGA and Genotype-Tissue Expression projects. Overall survival analysis was conducted using GEPIA2 plots of Kaplan-Meier curves. p-Values were computed using log-rank statistics. Hazard ratios (HRs) were calculated using the Cox proportional hazards model. The 95% confidence intervals are shown as dashed lines, and times were measured in months. Logrank p-values of ≤0.05 or HR p-values of ≤0.05 were considered statistically significant.

div.head: Results
div.p: Screening for overlapping DEGs between glioblastoma and normal brain tissues. In this work, we obtained the GSE12657, GSE50161, and GSE147352 datasets by searching for glioblastoma-related microarray or RNA-seq data using the keywords glioma, brain tumor, and glioblastoma in the NCBI GEO database. To screen for DEGs, we used GEO2R with the cutoff criteria adjusted p-value <0.05 and |log 2 FC| >2.0. We identified a total of 1,132 DEGs in GSE12657, of which 446 were up-regulated and 686 were down-regulated (Figure 1A). We also identified a total of 2,126 DEGs in GSE50161, of which 877 were up-regulated and 1,249 were down-regulated (Figure 1B). Finally, we identified a total of 4,041 DEGs in GSE147352, of which 2,133 were up-regulated, and 1,908 were down-regulated (Figure 1C). In the volcano plot, red dots represent up-regulated genes, and blue dots represent down-regulated genes based on an adjusted p-value <0.05 and |log 2 FC| >2.0. DEGs were then analyzed using a Venn diagram, and 439 DEGs (176 up-regulated and 263 downregulated) were found to overlap (Figure 1D and E). These common DEGs were selected for further analysis.

div.head: Functional enrichment analyses of overlapping DEGs in glioblastoma.
div.p: To understand the biological processes and pathways involved in the overlapping DEGs and to identify the pathways that cause diseases, overlapping DEGs were divided into up-regulated and down-regulated groups. GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses were then performed using DAVID. GO enrichment analysis showed 'cell division' (20 genes, p=2.01E-09) was the most significantly up-regulated 'Biological Process' among the up-regulated DEGs. Other important 'Biological Processes' associated with these upregulated DEGs were 'angiogenesis' (16 genes, p=6.97E-09), 'mitotic spindle assembly checkpoint' (8 genes, p=1.17E-08), 'collagen fibril organization' (10 genes, p=2.35E-08), and 'extracellular matrix organization' (13 genes, p=1.09E-07). For 'Cellular Components', the up-regulated DEGs were primarily related to 'extracellular space' (65 genes, p=2.41E-22), 'extracellular region' (67 genes, p=7.85E-22), 'extracellular exosome' (59 genes, p=2.37E-15), 'extracellular matrix' (21 genes, p=1.00E-13), and 'basement membrane' (13 genes, p=3.30E-11). For 'Molecular Functions', the up-regulated DEGs were particularly related to 'extracellular matrix structural constituent' (18 genes, p=1.25E-14), 'collagen binding' (12 genes, p=2.55E-11), 'protein binding' (150 genes, p=2.49E-08), 'protease binding' (10 genes, p=7.80E-07), and 'receptor binding' (16 genes, p=6.24E-06) (Figure 2A). Taken together, up-regulated DEGs were mainly involved in cell growth and proliferation, maintenance of cell structure, and regulation of cell function. Down-regulated DEGs for 'Biological Processes' showed significant enrichment in 'chemical synaptic transmission' (42 genes, p=5.21E-33), 'regulation of synaptic vesicle exocytosis' (12 genes, p=1.53E-10), 'signal transduction' (46 genes, p=4.65E-10), 'brain development' (20 genes, p=1.41E-09), and the 'gammaaminobutyric acid signaling pathway' (9 genes, p=1.78E-09). For 'Cellular Components', down-regulated DEGs were predominantly associated with the 'glutamatergic synapse' (53 genes, p=4.91E-37), 'neuron projection' (46 genes, p=1.87E-31), 'axon' (41 genes, p=1.24E-26), 'synapse' (47 genes, p=1.49E-25), and 'postsynaptic density' (32 genes, p=1.83E-21). For 'Molecular Functions', down-regulated DEGs were involved in 'calcium ion binding' (36 genes, p=9.77E-11), 'calmodulin binding' (19 genes, p=2.88E-10), 'neurotransmitter receptor activity' (10 genes, p=1.55E-06), 'chloride channel activity' (9 genes, p=2.86E-06), and 'GABA-A receptor activity' (6 genes, p=3.95E-06) (Figure 2B). Therefore, downregulated DEGs were mainly involved in the transmission of signals between neurons essential for brain function. KEGG analysis results showed that up-regulated DEGs were predominantly enriched in 'Cell cycle' (14 genes, p=9.35E-09), 'ECM-receptor interaction' (12 genes, p=1.69E-08), 'Focal adhesion' (15 genes, p=3.29E-07), 'AGE-RAGE signaling pathway in diabetic complications' (11 genes, p=6.61E-07), and 'PI3K-Akt signaling pathway' (17 genes, p=1.39E-05) (Figure 2C). Collectively, up-regulated DEGs were associated with signaling pathways that promote cell growth and proliferation, which contribute to cancer development and progression. Down-regulated DEGs were mostly enriched in 'Insulin secretion' (17 genes, p=1.83E-13), 'Long-term potentiation' (15 genes, p=1.20E-12), 'Glutamatergic synapse' (18 genes, p=1.36E-12), 'Calcium signaling pathway' (24 genes, p=1.67E-12) and 'Morphine addiction' (16 genes, p=6.92E-12) (Figure 2D). Therefore, down-regulated DEGs were associated with signaling pathways that play critical roles in nervous system function, and down-regulation of these pathways could lead to nervous system dysfunction.

div.head: Identification of hub genes associated with glioblastoma.
div.p: The 176 up-regulated and 263 down-regulated genes were entered into the STRING database to identify important protein-protein interactions. Results were then presented using Cytoscape software. In total, 408 nodes and 3,194 edges were displayed in the PPI network (Figure 3A). Next, the Cytoscape plugin cytoHubba was employed to identify hub genes. To achieve this, genes that appeared in the intersection of at least 8 of the top 10 genes identified by each of the 11 topology analysis methods were selected as glioblastoma-related hub genes. As a result, 4 downregulated genes, namely, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II alpha (CAMK2A), discs large MAGUK scaffold protein 4 (DLG4), synaptosome-associated protein 25 (SNAP25), and synaptotagmin 1 (SYT1) and 3 upregulated genes MYC proto-oncogene, bHLH transcription factor (MYC), fibronectin 1 (FN1), and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) were identified as hub genes (Figure 3B). In addition, these 7 hub genes were uploaded to GeneMANIA to predict genes with similar functional characteristics. As a result, 20 genes that formed a network, such as 'Physical Interaction', 'Co-expression', 'Pathway', 'Co-localization', 'Predicted', and 'Genetic Interactions', with hub genes emerged. This network was found to be involved in various functions related to neurotransmitters and tumorigenesis, including 'presynapse', 'neurotransmitter

Additional analysis was performed to determine the clinical significance of the 7 hub genes.

Expression and survival analyses of the hub genes. To examine the prognostic potential of the 7 hub genes, we initially compared the expression levels of these genes in glioblastoma samples and non-tumor samples using Gliovis. The expression levels of CAMK2A, DLG4, SNAP25, and SYT1 were found to be down-regulated in glioblastoma samples versus non-tumor brain samples (Figure 4A-D). On the other hand, MYC, FN1, and VEGFA were up-regulated in glioblastoma samples (Figure 4E-G). Also, overall survival analysis of the 7 hub genes using GEPIA2 showed that CAMK2A, DLG4, SNAP25, SYT1, and MYC were not significantly associated with the overall survival of glioblastoma patients (Figure 5A-E). However, FN1 and VEGFA were significantly associated with a decrease in the overall survival rate (Figure 5F and G). Additionally, survival analysis using gene signatures revealed a significant association between FN1 and VEGFA and decreased survival rates (Figure 5H). These findings indicate that FN1 and VEGFA might have potential use as prognostic markers for monitoring disease progression and predicting survival outcomes in glioblastoma.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: In the present study, the GSE12657, GSE50161, and GSE147352 datasets were comprehensively analyzed, and 439 significantly overlapped DEGs were identified. The results showed that 176 of these genes were up-regulated and 263 were down-regulated. GO analysis of the up-regulated genes showed that they were enriched in functions related to 'collagen fibril organization', 'extracellular space', and 'extracellular matrix structural constituent', which suggests that up-regulated genes primarily affected genes related to the extracellular matrix (ECM) and might be involved in glioblastoma development (29,30). The down-regulated genes were enriched primarily with functions related to 'chemical synaptic transmission', 'glutamatergic synapse', 'gamma-aminobutyric acid signaling pathway', and 'GABA-A receptor activity', which suggests that neurotransmitters might affect the development of tumors and cell proliferation and migration (31,32). Neurotransmitters synthesized by neurons and released into the synaptic cleft upon activation play a crucial role in the growth and invasion of glioblastoma (33). Glutamate is one of these neurotransmitters and promotes the growth of glioblastoma cells, while gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptors, a type of inhibitory neurotransmitter receptor, are expressed in

div.p: glioblastoma cells, and their activation has been shown to prevent glioblastoma cell invasion and growth (34,35). Our KEGG pathway enrichment analysis results showed that several pathways play important roles in the tumorigenesis of glioblastoma. The 'ECM-receptor interaction' includes a complex series of events that transmit signals from the ECM to cells and is important for many cellular processes, including adhesion, migration, and differentiation. Glioblastoma cells are able to interact with ECM in a way that promotes their growth and invasion (36). Furthermore, the 'PI3K-Akt signaling pathway' tends to be excessively activated in glioblastoma cells, and aberrant activation of this pathway promotes tumor growth and survival, and resistance to anticancer therapies (37,38).

In the present study, a PPI network was visualized using STRING and Cytoscape to screen hub genes, and then, CAMK2A, DLG4, SNAP25, SYT1, MYC, FN1, and VEGFA were focused on the network selected by cytoHubba. These hub genes are thought to be important for PPI network functioning and could be potential therapeutic targets. Then, using GeneMANIA, the 7 hub genes with 20 associated genes (ADAM8, BCAT1, CPLX1, FLT1, GRIK1, GRIN2B, KDR, LYVE1, NLGN4X, NRP2, PGF, RIMS1, SLC17A7, SLC18A2, SLC18A3, SV2A, SV2C, SYT2, SYT5, and UNC13B) were identified as being involved in biological functions related to neurotransmitters and tumorigenesis. The 'presynapse' and 'neurotransmitter transport' are crucial for the release and transport of neurotransmitters. The release of neurotransmitters from activated neurons into the synaptic cleft plays a key role in promoting the growth and invasion of glioblastoma (33). The 'regulation of angiogenesis' is crucial for supplying the nutrients and oxygen necessary for tumor growth, and the 'positive regulation of cell migration' facilitates the proliferation of tumor cells (39,40). The 'developmental growth' plays a role in tumor malignancy by driving uncontrolled cell proliferation, and the 'epithelial cell proliferation' supports the growth and survival of tumor cells (40). Additionally, the 'cell-substrate adhesion' facilitates tumor progression by increasing the motility and invasiveness of tumor cells (41). These functions are essential for the development of brain tumors, as they regulate the metabolism, signaling pathways, cellular homeostasis, and synaptic transmission in brain tumor cells. After screening hub genes, gene expression analysis and survival analysis were performed to determine the clinical significances of these genes. Gene expression analysis results confirmed that CAMK2A, DLG4, SNAP25, and SYT1 were down-regulated in glioblastoma samples, whereas MYC, FN1, and VEGFA were up-regulated. Survival analysis indicated that of the 7 hub genes, only FN1 and VEGFA were significantly associated with a poor prognosis, which suggests biological processes involving FN1 and VEGFA may participate in glioblastoma progression.

FN1 is a glycoprotein present in ECM and contributes to cell adhesion, proliferation, migration, and differentiation (42) and is abundant in basement membranes that form part of the blood-brain barrier around blood vessels (43). Furthermore, FN1 stimulates the invasiveness of glioblastoma cells (44,45), and its overexpression in glioblastoma has been reported to be associated with a poor prognosis (46). Several studies have shown FN1 contributes to the chemoresistance of various tumors, including glioblastoma (47,48), and it has been reported that the interaction between FN1 and β1-integrin receptor activates a signaling pathway that promotes cell survival, inhibits apoptosis, and thus, confers resistance to cancer chemotherapy-induced cell death and cell adhesion-mediated drug resistance in glioblastoma (48,49). Another study demonstrated that glioblastoma-derived cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) facilitate the migration and invasion of malignant cells, with CAF-derived FN1 contributing to the enhanced migratory and invasive phenotype (50). FN1 to integrin binding initiates signaling pathways that involve survival regulators, such as integrin-linked kinase, Akt, and NF-ĸB, and thus, facilitates cancer cell adhesion, growth, migration, and invasion (51). Also, recent research indicates FN1 contributes to radioresistance by interacting with ECM in response to radiation and activating signaling pathways that promote cell growth and cell survival (52). Furthermore, FN1 increased the radioresistance of glioblastoma stem cells (the main cell type in glioblastoma) by repairing DNA damage, inhibiting apoptosis, and increasing antioxidant activity (53). Taken together, it appears FN1 increases the ability of cancer cells to survive chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Thus, targeting FN1 would be expected to increase the survival of cancer patients.

VEGFA (also called VEGF) is a member of the VEGF gene family and a representative pro-angiogenic factor (39). Several studies have reported that VEGFA is up-regulated in various cancers, including lung cancer, renal clear cell carcinoma, and glioblastoma (54)(55)(56). Furthermore, glioblastoma is characterized by a high degree of angiogenesis (57,58), and VEGFA stimulates cancer cells to form new blood vessels and provides an environment that enables cancer cells to grow and metastasize (59). VEGFA is also known to promote endothelial cell proliferation and migration and to increase vascular permeability (60). Glioblastoma is characterized by the overexpression of VEGF through hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, which promotes vascular growth, and thus, promoting glioblastoma proliferation and metastasis (61,62). Also, VEGFA positively regulates matrix metalloproteinase 2 (MMP2), which promotes the invasion and metastasis of glioblastoma via the ERK/MAPK pathway. MMP2 can break down ECM, and thus, helps tumor cells invade surrounding tissues and metastasize (63,64). Therefore, the effective targeting of VEGFA may be an important strategy in the treatment of glioblastoma (65).

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this study, multiple bioinformatics analyses showed that FN1 and VEGFA are significantly related to the tumorigenesis and progression of glioblastoma. Specifically, these genes appear to increase blood supply to tumor cells by increasing angiogenesis. Based on our findings, we propose that FN1 and VEGFA could be potential therapeutic targets for glioblastoma treatment. However, a limitation of our study is that our analysis mainly used bioinformatics data, which may not fully reflect the complexities of the tumor microenvironment and interactions between different cell types. To overcome this limitation, future studies should use in vivo models to confirm the roles of FN1 and VEGFA in the progression of glioblastoma. These studies should also include experiments that either knock out or overexpress these genes to understand better how they specifically contribute. Nonetheless, our findings suggest novel means of determining the prognosis of glioblastoma and detecting the disease at an early stage.
